For over 150 years a small tetra has been known in science that is placed, because of the scalation of the tail fin, in the genus Moenkhausia under the name M. lepidura. The species was thought to differ from all other Moenkhausia species by the coloration of the tail fin, in the upper half of which there is a black spot, while the lower half is colourless.

Only in 2016 did Marinho & Langeani show that there are several species with this pattern. They found that the "real" M. lepidura can be recognised by a special feature in the scalation. On the back of M. lepidura the edges of the scales of the flanks meet directly against each other (like a house of cards), while in other, similar species an additional row of scales forms a ridge, so to speak. This can be seen well in a photo in which the fish is taken frontally.

A Moenkhausia species of this species complex was received from Colombia that cannot be M. lepidura because of its back scalation. Following the identification key of Marinho & Langeani, it is most probably M. celibela, but there is also much similarity to M. mikia. It can never be completely ruled out that this is a scientifically not yet recorded, new species.

These fish are also extremely similar in colour to a scientifically undescribed Bryconops species from the Rio Xingu in Brazil. However, Bryconops species have long anal fins, comparatively larger eyes and a completely different swimming behaviour.

Marinho, M. M., & F. Langeani (2016). Reconciling more than 150 years of taxonomic confusion: the true identity of Moenkhausia lepidura, with a key to the species of the M. lepidura group (Characiformes: Characidae). Zootaxa, 4107 (3), 338-352.
